questions.prompt: `./prog a b c` is run. What are `argc` and `argv[2]`?
questions.explain: `argv[0]` is the program name, so there are 4 entries: `./prog`, `a`, `b`, `c`. `argv[2]` is `"b"`.
option_notes: argc counts the program name too.

questions.prompt: Which `main` signature also receives the environment variables?
options: int main(int argc, char *argv[], int envc)
questions.explain: Unix (as a common extension) passes a third parameter, a NULL-terminated array of `"NAME=value"` strings. `getenv("NAME")` is the portable way to read one variable.

questions.prompt: The program is started as `./prog -v file.txt`. What are `argc` and `argv[1]`?
questions.explain: `argv[0]` is the program name, so there are 3 entries: `./prog`, `-v`, `file.txt`.
The standard guarantees that `argv[argc]` is a null pointer, so you can also walk the array until you hit NULL.
options: NULL (the array is terminated by a null pointer)
option_notes: It is a null pointer, not a string.

questions.prompt: The user types `./prog "a b" c`. How many arguments does the program receive?
questions.explain: The shell removes the quotes and passes `a b` as a single argument. So argv has `./prog`, `a b` and `c`: argc is 3, i.e. 2 real arguments.
option_notes: Quoted text is not split at the space.
There are two arguments after the program name.

questions.prompt: The user types `./prog *.c` in a directory with `a.c` and `b.c`. What does the program receive?
questions.explain: The SHELL expands wildcards before starting the program. Quote the pattern (`'*.c'`) to receive it unexpanded.
options: Two arguments: a.c and b.c (the shell expands the pattern)
option_notes: Only if the pattern is quoted or nothing matches.

questions.prompt: Why is `strtol` better than `atoi` for converting an argument to a number?
questions.explain: `atoi("abc")` returns 0, the same as `atoi("0")`, with no way to tell. `strtol` sets an end pointer (and `errno` on overflow).
options: It tells you where the conversion stopped, so you can detect invalid text
option_notes: It can fail; you check the end pointer.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (`strtol` and its end pointer.)
questions.explain: `strtol` converts the leading `42` and leaves `end` pointing at the first character it could not use, `abc`.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (Nothing to convert.)
questions.explain: With no digits `strtol` returns 0 and sets `end` to the start of the string: `end == s` is how you detect that nothing was converted.
`getenv` returns NULL for a variable that does not exist, so always test the result before using it.

questions.prompt: The number the program returns from `main` is its {{0}} status; 0 means success.
questions.explain: The shell shows it in `$?`; a non-zero value signals failure.

questions.prompt: Which statements about `main(int argc, char *argv[], char *envp[])` are true?
questions.explain: `argv[0]` is the program name; the user's first argument is `argv[1]`. All arguments are strings: convert numbers with `strtol`.
options: `envp` is an array of `NAME=value` strings ended by NULL
`getenv` is the portable way to read one variable
`argv[0]` is the first argument the user typed after the program name
Every argument is passed as a string
